items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: And of course the Basie saxophone section with Earle Warren, Tab Smith, Don Byas, or Buddy Tate and Lester Young.

ctx.x: So you saw some of the great saxophone sections coming through there.

Yes, yes. Benny Carter had a — oh my goodness, he had a lead alto player named Porter Kilbourn who was almost as ferocious as he himself was. And of course the great Duke Ellington had Johnny Hodges and Otto Hardwick and Harry Carney. And of course the Basie saxophone section with Earle Warren, Tab Smith, Don Byas, or Buddy Tate and Lester Young.
So you got to hear Lester in the Basie band?

items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: After he left Basie’s band he came back to Ohio and formed a band of his own and hired me as a kid to play with him for a few months.

ctx.x: I’ll start with the local bands. As I said before, the principal concentration of music, jazz, was in the west end, downtown Cincinnati. One of the bands down there was a band that was rehearsing at what was called the 9th Street YMCA. Now this band didn’t have a name, and it never ever played a job, but I went down there to rehearse with this band, and I made connections with Jack Jackson’s Jumping Jacks, which were -- their home base was the west end. Also there was another very good band, Andrew Johnson’s big…

Right around the corner from there was that principal area of jazz music activity in the black community, Cincinnati’s Cotton Club. They had a house band, stage shows, comedians, singers, dancers, a chorus line, all that, the whole bit in the Cotton Club. The house band was led by a tenor saxophonist whose name was A. B. Townsend. He would remind one -- in his approach to playing and his sound would remind one of Gene Ammons, the late Gene Ammons. These were the quality musicians that we had around there. Then in…
What was Covington? Was Covington an open city too?
